question: I want to measure the distance between two Bluetooth devices (A Master and a slave) using the corresponding RSSI value. Is there any algorithm or popular approach that maps RSSI values directly to distance?

sections.title: Fundamentals of RSSI Measurement
sections.text: Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) represents the actual signal power detected by a receiver, typically quantified in decibel milliwatts (dBm) [1]. This metric enables distance estimation between a transmitter and receiver by analyzing the difference between the transmitted and received signal powers [1]. While multipath propagation is generally regarded as an obstacle to accurate distance determination , small-scale fading offers a highly sensitive measure of location, capable of detecting movement on the order of a wavelength.

sections.title: Propagation Models for Distance Conversion
sections.text: Geometric approaches calculate distances from RSSI values by applying an adequate mathematical model [1]. Two primary propagation models are generally used to convert RSSI to distance: free-space models and log-normal models [1][1]. In a pure free-space scenario, the path loss power is proportional to the square of the distance (d) between the transmitter and receiver [2]. More generally, this loss can be modeled as d^n_PL, where the pathloss coefficient n_PL depends on the specific environment and line-of-sight conditions [2]. The free-space path loss equation relates received power (P_RX) to transmitted power (P_TX), antenna gains (G_TX, G_RX), wavelength (λ), and distance (d). question: In recommendation systems, how are new methods that optimize diversity typically evaluated?

sections.title: Multifaceted Evaluation Frameworks
sections.text: Evaluating recommender systems is a complex, multifaceted process that extends beyond measuring a few key metrics of a single model, as these systems have far-reaching impacts on user experiences. Consequently, performance should be assessed not only by accuracy but also by diversity and novelty [3]. Recent surveys propose unified taxonomies to classify diversification metrics and approaches in search and recommendation. These frameworks review the latest research progress, expounding on multiple perspectives such as accuracy, diversity, and novelty, while conducting in-depth analyses of the advantages, disadvantages, and applicable environments of various evaluation metrics [2][2]. Specifically, some reviews focus on three levels of recommended diversity and their corresponding evaluation criteria [2]. The inclusion of diversity, novelty, and serendipity in evaluation is supported by findings that these approaches, which are orthogonal to traditional accuracy-based measures, increase user satisfaction [1].

sections.title: Metric Taxonomies and Relevance-Awareness
sections.text: Surveys classify relevance-aware diversity metrics into distinct sub-classes and maintain lookup tables to determine their applicability in search versus recommendation contexts. A common distinction is made between relevance-oblivious and relevance-aware metrics. Specific metric families include P-Coverage (system-level), NRBP, nDCU@K, M-IA (IA-family), and D-M/D#-M (D-family). The D/D#-metrics are notable for combining traditional ranking quality metrics, such as nDCG, MRR, and MAP, with the diversity measure D-M@K via a parameter gamma. Key references in this area include the rank-biased utility metric by Amigó et al. (SIGIR 2018), Hurley's work on diverse recommendation (DiveRS@RecSys 2011), and DPP-based diversity by Chen et al. (NIPS 2018). P-Coverage focuses on the system level and is hardly used for single ranking lists, though it relates to the cold-start problem.

sections.title: Computational Methods for Diversity
sections.text: Most methods proposed to evaluate diversity use item-item similarity based on item content to form item neighborhoods, then measure the min, max, sum, or average distance between pairs of items [6]. An alternative approach involves measuring the value of inserting a new item to the list of recommendation, a method utilized by Ziegler et al. [6]. For aggregate diversity, Adomavicius and Kwon used the total number of different items recommended across all users as a measure to evaluate the recommendation algorithm [6]. However, systems that optimize for user- or item-level diversity do not necessarily score well in system-level diversity, motivating the need for a new objective that combines all of these considerations [5]. Proposed diversification scenarios have been shown to improve diversity measures in session-based recommender systems based on four news datasets [4].

question: In robotics, what are the leading methods for learning terrain traversibility costs automatically from robot experience?

sections.title: Experiential Learning Frameworks
sections.text: A primary approach to automatic terrain cost estimation involves learning directly from a robot's prior navigation history. This experience-based methodology allows robots to autonomously determine which terrains are traversable without relying on external data sources [3][3]. The core premise is that accurately estimating a terrain's actual cost is difficult until the robot has physically traversed it, making the accumulation of previous experience essential [2]. This paradigm addresses robotic navigation by learning how to traverse real-world environments using real-world data [1]. The process operates on two levels: a low level that deals with local traversibility and a high level that determines which paths are more likely to lead to the destination [1].

sections.text: Several methods characterize traversability through the robot's internal physical state rather than external visual cues. Faigl and Prágr utilize robot proprioceptive features to characterize three specific traversal costs: mean instantaneous power consumption, mean forward velocity, and attitude stability [5]. These internal metrics are attached to exteroceptive features for regression purposes [5]. In a related ground-vehicle study, self-organizing maps are proposed to predict these same three traversal costs—instantaneous power consumption, maximum achievable forward velocity, and attitude stability—based on terrain morphology and appearance from an RGB-D camera [4]. During the learning phase, the predicting model is fed with the traversal costs actually experienced by the robot during traversal [4]. sections.title: Theoretical Framework and Hypotheses
sections.text: The Temporal Response Function (TRF) is a functionally informative statistic derived from a linear model that predicts neural responses to sound stimuli [6]. It operates as a linear transfer function describing the relationship between specific speech features and the resulting neural activity [4] [5]. This methodology originates from system identification techniques [3]. The core hypothesis posits that ascending brain processing stages exhibit emergent features, progressing from acoustic to sentence-level linguistic representations as incremental steps in speech processing [2]. The TRF is a continuous signal that exhibits neural encoding of speech features over time, typically spanning hundreds of milliseconds [2]. Peaks of different latencies within this signal indicate separate processing stages [2]. By mapping the envelope to EEG across various time lags, the TRF yields peaks similar to event-related potentials obtained for auditory stimuli [1]. This approach is particularly useful for studying the segmentation of speech, where the temporal envelope is mapped onto neural electroencephalographic data [1].

sections.text: The Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem establishes that the sampling frequency must be at least twice the maximum frequency of the signal to be recorded [3]. Consequently, sampling at a frequency of ω_sample limits the obtainable information to a frequency band of width Δω_FFT = ω_sample/2 [2]. In practical applications, this principle dictates that the minimum required sampling frequency is 2.0 Hz, which corresponds to a maximum allowed sampling period of 0.5 s [1].
